newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish high growth may lead to inflation woes - OECD.
newsitem.headline: Irish high growth may lead to inflation woes - OECD.

text.p: The Organisation of Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) expects Ireland's growth rate to remain robust but warns that inflation pressures may start to rise.

The OECD, in its June Economic Outlook report on Thursday, projected Ireland's growth to remain buoyant in 1997 and 1998, supported by the rapid increase in the labour force and the sustained inflow of foreign investment.

It said Ireland's Gross National Product will remain close to 6.0 percent in 1997 and 1998 and Ireland's gross government debt is expected to decline to 69 percent in 1997, down from 82 percent in 1995.
"Rapid economic growth will ... continue to reduce the public debt ratio, however, inflation pressure may start to rise," the report warned.
Ireland's strong expansion should generate continued employment gains that could reduce the unemployment rate to below 11 percent in 1997, the OECD said.
It said this may lead to a slight pick-up in both wage and price inflation.
"With employment expected to expand more than three percent annually during the next two years, the unemployment rate may fall to under 11 percent," the OECD said.

It said the large inflow of foreign investment in 1996 was expected to sustain export growth, while the prospects for European Economic and Monetary Union membership may lead to declines in interest rates which will support domestic demand.
The OECD warned that there was a risk of a further decline in the saving rate in the context of rising asset prices and improved labour market conditions.
"This would add to demand pressures and increase the risk of inflation," the OECD said.
Fiscal policy continues to aim for a progressive reduction in the burden of debt by keeping the budget deficit low, while reducing the tax burden to improve work incentives, the report said.
It said Ireland's 1997 budget sees a slight widening of the country's deficit to 1.5 percent of GDP from 0.9 percent in 1996.

"This reflects the government's acquiescence in allowing spending growth above the target of a 2.0 percent rise in real terms and the new central wage agreement, which grants tax cuts in exchange for limiting wage growth to less than 3.0 percent per year over the period 1997 to 1999."
Nevertheless, gross government debt is projected to decline to 69 percent in 1997 as the actual deficit seems likely to be lower than that envisagesd in the budget, it said.
